stem: A hose pipe used for gardening is ejecting water horizontally at the rate of \(0.5\) m/s. Area of the bore of the pipe is \(10\) cm\(^2\). Calculate the force to be applied by the gardener to hold the pipe horizontally stationary.
solution:
If ejecting water horizontally is considered as action force on the water, the water exerts a backward force (called recoil force) on the pipe as the reaction force.

\(\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \frac{d\left(m\vec{v}\right)}{dt} = \frac{dm}{dt}\vec{v} + m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}\)

As v, the velocity of ejected water is constant, \(F = \frac{dm}{dt}\vec{v}\), where \(\frac{dm}{dt}\) is the rate at which mass of water is ejected by the pipe.

As the force is in the direction of velocity (horizontal), we can use scalars.

\(\therefore F = \frac{dm}{dt}v\)

\(\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{d\left(V\rho\right)}{dt} = \frac{d\left(Al\rho\right)}{dt} = A\rho\frac{dl}{dt} = A\rho v\)

where \(V\) = volume of water ejected

\(A\) = area of cross section of bore = \(10\) cm\(^2\)

\(\rho\) = density of water = \(1\) g/cc

\(l\) = length of the water ejected in time \(t\)

\(\frac{dl}{dt} = v\) = velocity of water ejected = \(0.5\) m/s = \(50\) cm/s

\(F = \frac{dm}{dt}v = \left(A\rho v\right)v = A\rho v^2 = 10 \times 1 \times 50^2\)

\(= 25000\) dyne \(= 0.25\) N

Equal and opposite force must be applied by the gardener.
_note: Printed inconsistency (does NOT affect the answer): the line 'As v, the velocity of ejected water is constant' prints a scalar \(F\) equated to a vector \(\vec{v}\) term, i.e. \(F = \frac{dm}{dt}\vec{v}\). The book itself resolves this on the very next line ('we can use scalars') where it writes \(\therefore F = \frac{dm}{dt}v\). Transcribed as printed. Arithmetic verified: \(10 \times 1 \times 50^2 = 25000\) dyne \(= 0.25\) N (cgs units throughout).

stem: Three identical point masses are fixed symmetrically on the periphery of a circle. Obtain the resultant gravitational force on any point mass \(M\) at the centre of the circle. Extend this idea to more than three identical masses symmetrically located on the periphery. How far can you extend this concept?
solution:
(i) Figure below shows three identical point masses \(m\) on the periphery of a circle of radius \(r\). Mass \(M\) is at the centre of the circle. Gravitational forces on \(M\) due to these masses are attractive and are directed as shown.

In magnitude, \(F_{MA} = F_{MB} = F_{MC} = \frac{GMm}{r^2}\)

[Figure: a circle of radius \(r\) with centre \(M\). Three equal point masses \(m\) sit on the circumference at \(A\) (top), \(B\) (lower left) and \(C\) (lower right), spaced \(120^\circ\) apart. From \(M\) an arrow \(F_{MA}\) points up towards \(A\), an arrow \(F_{MB}\) points down-left towards \(B\) and an arrow \(F_{MC}\) points down-right towards \(C\). The resolved components are also drawn from \(M\): a horizontal arrow to the left labelled \(F_{MB}\cos 60^\circ\) and a horizontal arrow to the right labelled \(F_{MC}\sin 60^\circ\), together with two arrows pointing vertically downwards labelled \(F_{MB}\cos 60^\circ\) and \(F_{MC}\cos 60^\circ\).]

Forces \(F_{MB}\) and \(F_{MC}\) are resolved along \(F_{MA}\) and perpendicular to \(F_{MA}\) as shown. Components perpendicular to \(F_{MA}\) cancel each other. Components along \(F_{MA}\) are \(F_{MB}\cos 60^\circ = F_{MC}\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}F_{MA}\) each. Magnitude of their resultant is \(F_{MA}\) and its direction is opposite to that of \(F_{MA}\). Thus, the resultant force on mass \(M\) is zero.

(ii) For any even number of equal masses, the force due to any mass \(m\) is balanced (cancelled) by diametrically opposite mass. For any odd number of masses, as seen for 3, the components perpendicular to one of them cancel each other while the components parallel to one of these add up in such a way that the resultant is zero for any number of identical masses \(m\) located symmetrically on the periphery.

(iii) As the number of masses tends to infinity, their collective shape approaches circumference of the circle, which is nothing but a ring. Thus, the gravitational force exerted by a ring mass on any other mass at its centre is zero.
diagramNote: Circle of radius r centred at M with three equal masses m at A (top), B (lower left), C (lower right), 120 degrees apart; attraction vectors F_MA (up), F_MB (down-left), F_MC (down-right) drawn from M, plus the two horizontal (perpendicular) components and the two downward components along the line opposite to F_MA.
_note: Figure label misprint (does NOT affect the printed conclusion): the LEFT horizontal arrow is labelled \(F_{MB}\cos 60^\circ\) while the RIGHT horizontal arrow — the equal and opposite component of the same magnitude — is labelled \(F_{MC}\sin 60^\circ\). Verified at high magnification on the page image: the left label reads 'cos', not 'sin'. Both horizontal components are perpendicular to \(F_{MA}\) and equal \(F\sin 60^\circ\), so the left label should read \(F_{MB}\sin 60^\circ\); as printed it is also self-contradictory within the same figure, since the two DOWNWARD components are (correctly) labelled \(F_{MB}\cos 60^\circ\) and \(F_{MC}\cos 60^\circ\). Transcribed as printed. The prose derivation and the result (resultant on \(M\) is zero) are correct.

stem: A car of mass \(1.5\) ton is running at \(72\) kmph on a straight horizontal road. On turning the engine off, it stops in \(20\) seconds. While running at the same speed, on the same road, the driver observes an accident \(50\) m in front of him. He immediately applies the brakes and just manages to stop the car at the accident spot. Calculate the braking force.
solution:
On turning the engine off,

\(u = 20\,\mathrm{m\ s}^{-1}\), \(v = 0\), \(t = 20\,s\)

\(\therefore a = \frac{v - u}{t} = -1\,\mathrm{m\ s}^{-2}\)

This is frictional retardation (negative acceleration).

After seeing the accident,

\(u = 20\,\mathrm{m\ s}^{-1}\), \(v = 0\), \(s = 50\,\mathrm{m}\)

\(\therefore a_1 = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2s} = -4\,\mathrm{m\ s}^{-2}\)

This retardation is the combined effect of braking and friction. Thus, braking retardation \(= 4 - 1 = 3\,\mathrm{m\ s}^{-2}\).

\(\therefore\) Braking force = mass \(\times\) braking retardation \(= 1500 \times 3 = 4500\) N
_note: Derivation checked and internally consistent: \(72\) kmph \(= 20\) m s\(^{-1}\); \(a = (0-20)/20 = -1\) m s\(^{-2}\); \(a_1 = (0-400)/(2\times 50) = -4\) m s\(^{-2}\); braking retardation \(3\) m s\(^{-2}\); \(1.5\) ton \(= 1500\) kg gives \(4500\) N.

stem: Over a given region, a force (in newton) varies as \(F = 3x^2 - 2x + 1\). In this region, an object is displaced from \(x_1 = 20\) cm to \(x_2 = 40\) cm by the given force. Calculate the amount of work done.
_note: Derivation checked and internally consistent: \(0.064 - 0.16 + 0.4 = 0.304\); \(0.008 - 0.04 + 0.2 = 0.168\); difference \(= 0.136\) J. The displacement limits are correctly converted from cm to m (\(20\) cm \(\to 0.2\), \(40\) cm \(\to 0.4\)) even though the stem states them in cm.

stem: Figure (a) shows a fixed pulley. A massless inextensible string with masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2 > m_1\) attached to its two ends is passing over the pulley. Such an arrangement is called an Atwood machine. Calculate accelerations of the masses and force due to the tension along the string assuming axle of the pulley to be frictionless.
solution:
[Fig. (a): a pulley fixed to a rigid support, with a string passing over it carrying the mass \(m_1\) hanging on the left and the mass \(m_2\) hanging on the right. The force due to tension \(T\) acts upwards along the string on each mass, while the weights \(m_1 g\) and \(m_2 g\) act vertically downwards.]

**Method I:** Direct method: As \(m_2 > m_1\), mass \(m_2\) is moving downwards and mass \(m_1\) is moving upwards.

Net downward force

\(= F = \left(m_2\right)g - \left(m_1\right)g = \left(m_2 - m_1\right)g\)

As the string is inextensible, both the masses travel the same distance in the same time. Thus, their accelerations are numerically the same (one upward, other downward). Let it be \(a\).

Thus, total mass in motion, \(M = m_2 + m_1\)

\(\therefore a = \dfrac{F}{M} = \left(\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_2 + m_1}\right)g\)

For mass \(m_1\), the upward force is the force due to tension \(T\) and downward force is \(mg\). It has upward acceleration \(a\). Thus, \(T - m_1 g = ma\)

\(\therefore T = m_1(g + a)\)

Using the expression for \(a\), we get

\(T = \left(\dfrac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)g\)

**Method II:** (Free body equations)

[Fig. (b) and Fig. (c): free body diagram of \(m_1\) - the force due to tension \(T\) acting vertically upwards and the weight \(m_1 g\) acting vertically downwards; free body diagram of \(m_2\) - the force due to tension \(T\) acting vertically upwards and the weight \(m_2 g\) acting vertically downwards.]

Free body diagrams of \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are as shown in Figs. (b) and (c).

Thus, for the first body, \(T - m_1 g = m_1 a\) --- (I)

For the second body, \(m_2 g - T = m_2 a\) --- (II)

Adding (I) and (II), and solving for \(a\),

we get, \(a = \left(\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_2 + m_1}\right)g\) --- (III)

Solving Eqs. (II) and (III) for \(T\), we get,

\(T = m_2(g - a) = \left(\dfrac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)g\)
diagramNote: Fig. (a) is the Atwood-machine setup (fixed pulley, string over it, m1 hanging left and m2 hanging right, tension T up on each mass, weights m1g and m2g down). Method II additionally prints two separate free body diagrams, one per mass, each showing T upwards and the weight downwards. The stem states the arrangement fully in words, so no step is unanswerable without the figures; they are the setup, not the answer.
_note: Two printed defects, neither answer-affecting. (1) In Method II BOTH figure captions are printed as "Fig. (b)" while the sentence immediately below them reads "Free body diagrams of m1 and m2 are as shown in Figs. (b) and (c)" - the second caption should read "Fig. (c)". (2) In Method I the book prints "downward force is mg" and "T - m_1 g = ma" using a bare m where m_1 is meant; the very next line correctly writes T = m_1(g + a). Both transcribed as printed. All three expressions for T were checked numerically and agree (m1(g+a) = m2(g-a) = 2m1m2 g/(m1+m2)).

stem: One marble collides head-on with another identical marble at rest. If the collision is partially inelastic, determine the ratio of their final velocities in terms of coefficient of restitution \(e\).
solution:
According to conservation of momentum, \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2\)

As \(m_1 = m_2\), we get, \(u_1 + u_2 = v_1 + v_2\)

\(\therefore\) If \(u_2 = 0\), we get, \(v_1 + v_2 = u_1\) ... (I)

Coefficient of restitution,

\(e = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}\)  \(\therefore v_2 - v_1 = e u_1\) ... (II)

Dividing Eq. (I) by Eq. (II),

\(\dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{v_2 - v_1} = \dfrac{1}{e}\)

Using componendo and dividendo, we get,

\(\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \dfrac{1 + e}{1 - e}\)

stem: A shell of mass 3 kg is dropped from some height. After falling freely for 2 seconds, it explodes into two fragments of masses 2 kg and 1 kg. Kinetic energy provided by the explosion is 300 J. Using \(g = 10 \text{ m/s}^{2}\), calculate velocities of the fragments. Justify your answer if you have more than one options.
solution:
\(m_1 + m_2 = 3\) kg.

After falling freely for 2 seconds,

\(v = u + at = 0 + 10(2) = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1} = u_1 = u_2\)

According to conservation of linear momentum, \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2\)

\(\therefore 3 \times 20 = 2v_1 + 1v_2\)  \(\therefore v_2 = 60 - 2v_1\) --- (I)

K.E. provided = Final K.E. \(-\) Initial K.E. \(= \dfrac{1}{2}m_1 v_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_2 v_2^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(m_1 + m_2\right)u^2\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{2}2v_1^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}v_2^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}3(20)^2 = 300 \text{ J}\)

or \(2v_1^2 + v_2^2 = 1800\)

or \(2v_1^2 + \left(60 - 2v_1\right)^2 = 1800\) using Eq. (I)

\(\therefore 3600 - 240v_1 + 6v_1^2 = 1800\)

\(\therefore v_1^2 - 40v_1 + 300 = 0\)

\(\therefore v_1 = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}\) or \(10 \text{ m s}^{-1}\) and

\(v_2 = 0\) or \(40 \text{ m s}^{-1}\)

There are two possible answers since the positions of two fragments can be different as explained below.

If \(v_1 = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}\) and \(v_2 = 0\), lighter fragment 2 should be above. On the other hand, if \(v_1 = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}\) and \(v_2 = 40 \text{ m s}^{-1}\), lighter fragment 2 should be below, both moving downwards.

stem: Bullets of mass 40 g each, are fired from a machine gun at a rate of 5 per second towards a firmly fixed hard surface of area \(10 \text{ cm}^{2}\). Each bullet hits normal to the surface at 400 m/s and rebounds in such a way that the coefficient of restitution for the collision between bullet and the surface is 0.75. Calculate average force and average pressure experienced by the surface due to this firing.
solution:
For the collision,

\(u_1 = 400 \text{ m s}^{-1}\), \(e = 0.75\), \(v_1 = ?\)

For the firmly fixed hard surface, \(u_2 = v_2 = 0\)

\(e = 0.75 = \dfrac{v_1 - v_2}{u_2 - u_1} = \dfrac{v_1 - 0}{0 - 400}\)  \(\therefore v_1 = -300\) m/s.

-ve sign indicates that the bullet rebounds in exactly opposite direction.

Change in momentum of each bullet \(= m\left(v_1 - u_1\right)\)

Equal and opposite will be the momentum transferred to the surface, per collision.

\(\therefore\) Momentum transferred to the surface, per collision

\(p = m\left(u_1 - v_1\right) = 0.04\left(400 - \left[-300\right]\right) = 28 \text{ N s}\)

The rate of collision is same as rate of firing.

\(\therefore\) Momentum received by the surface per second, \(\dfrac{dp}{dt} = 28 \times 5 = 140 \text{ N}\)

This must be the average force experienced by the surface of area \(A = 10 \text{ cm}^{2} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) Average pressure experienced,

\(P = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{140}{10^{-3}} = 1.4 \times 10^{5} \text{ N m}^{-2}\)

\(\approx 1.4\) times the atmospheric pressure.

stem: Mass of an Oxygen molecule is \(5.35 \times 10^{-26}\) kg and that of a Nitrogen molecule is \(4.65 \times 10^{-26}\) kg. During their Brownian motion (random motion) in air, an Oxygen molecule travelling with a velocity of 400 m/s collides elastically with a nitrogen molecule travelling with a velocity of 500 m/s in the exactly opposite direction. Calculate the impulse received by each of them during collision. Assuming that the collision lasts for 1 ms, how much is the average force experienced by each molecule?
solution:
Let

\(m_1 = m_{\text{O}} = 5.35 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}\),

\(m_2 = m_{\text{N}} = 4.65 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}\).

\(\therefore u_1 = 400\ \text{m s}^{-1}\ \text{and}\ u_2 = -500\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

taking direction of motion of Oxygen molecule as the positive direction.

For an elastic collision,

\(v_1 = \left(\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \left(\dfrac{2m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2\)  and

\(v_2 = \left(\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2 + \left(\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1\)

\(\therefore v_1 = -437\ \text{m s}^{-1}\ \text{and}\ v_2 = 463\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore J_{\text{O}} = m_{\text{O}}\left(v_1 - u_1\right) = -4.478 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{N s}\),

\(J_{\text{N}} = m_{\text{N}}\left(v_2 - u_2\right) = +4.478 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{N s}\)

As expected, the net impulse or net change in momentum is zero.

\(F_{\text{ON}} = \dfrac{dp_{\text{O}}}{dt} = \dfrac{J_{\text{O}}}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{-4.478 \times 10^{-23}}{10^{-3}}\)

\(= -4.478 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{N}\)

and \(F_{\text{NO}} = -F_{\text{ON}} = 4.478 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{N}\)
_note: The book prints NO 'Solution' label for this example. The worked solution begins directly after the question with the word 'Let'. Every step of the printed derivation was checked and is internally consistent (v1 = -437, v2 = +463, J = 4.478e-23 N s, F = 4.478e-20 N).

stem: A uniform wooden plank of mass 30 kg is supported symmetrically by two light identical cables; each can sustain a tension up to 500 N. After tying, the cables are exactly vertical and are separated by 2 m. A boy of mass 50 kg, standing at the centre of the plank, is interested in walking on the plank. How far can he walk? \((g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2})\)
solution:
Let \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) be the tensions along the cables, both acting vertically upwards.

[Figure: the plank hangs from a ceiling by two vertical cables carrying tensions \(T_1\) (left) and \(T_2\) (right), whose points of attachment on the plank are 2 m apart. The centre of the plank is marked 1 m from the left cable; the 300 N weight of the plank acts downwards there, and the boy's 500 N weight acts downwards at the point where he stands.]

Weight of the plank 300 N is acting vertically downwards through the centre, 1 m from either cable. Weight of the boy, 500 N is vertically downwards at the point where he is standing.

\(\therefore T_1 + T_2 = 300 + 500 = 800\ \text{N}\)

Suppose that the boy is able to walk \(x\) m towards the right. Obviously, the tension in the right side cable goes on increasing as he walks towards the cable.

Moments of 300 N and 500 N forces about left end A are clockwise, while that of \(T_2\) is anticlockwise.

As the cable can sustain 500 N, \(\left(T_2\right)_{\text{max}} = 500\ \text{N}\)

Thus, for the equilibrium about A, we can write,

\(300 \times 1 + 500 \times \left(1 + x\right) = 500 \times 2\)  \(\therefore x = 0.4\ \text{m}\)

Thus, the boy can walk up to 40 cm on either side of the centre.
diagramNote: Plank suspended from a ceiling by two vertical cables 2 m apart (tensions T1 and T2); 1 m mark from the left cable to the plank's centre; downward 300 N (plank) and 500 N (boy) arrows.
_note: The printed solution takes moments 'about left end A', but the point A is NOT labelled anywhere in the accompanying figure (the figure labels only T1, T2, 2m, 1m, 300N, 500N). From the moment equation (the T2 arm is 2 m) A is evidently the attachment point of the LEFT CABLE, not the left end of the plank. The arithmetic is internally consistent: 300 + 500(1+x) = 1000 gives x = 0.4 m.

stem: A ladder of negligible mass having a cross bar is resting on a frictionless horizontal floor with angle between its legs to be \(40^\circ\). Each leg is 1 m long. Calculate the force experienced by the cross bar when a person of mass 50 kg is standing on the ladder. \((g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2})\)
solution:
Tension \(T\) along the cross bar is horizontal. Let \(L\) be the length of each leg, which is 1 m.

[Figure: the ladder is drawn as an inverted V (A-frame) standing on the floor, the two legs meeting at the apex with the \(40^\circ\) angle between them. The weight \(W\) of the person acts vertically downwards at the apex. A horizontal cross bar joins the two legs part-way down and is shown pulling inwards on each leg with tension \(T\). Vertical normal reactions \(N\) act upwards at the two feet.]

As there is no friction, there is no horizontal reaction at the floor. Reaction \(N\) given by the floor at the base of the ladder will then be only vertical. Thus, along the vertical, two such reactions balance weight \(W = mg\) of the person.

\(\therefore N = \dfrac{mg}{2} = 250\ \text{N}\)

At the left leg, about the upper end, the torque due to \(N\) is clockwise and that due to the tension \(T\) is anticlockwise. For equilibrium, these two torques should have same magnitude.

\(\therefore N.L\sin 20^\circ = T.\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)\cos 20^\circ\)

\(\therefore T = 2N\tan 20^\circ = 2 \times 250 \times 0.364 = 182\ \text{N}\)
diagramNote: A-frame ladder on a horizontal floor, 40 degrees between the legs; weight W down at the apex, horizontal cross bar with inward tensions T at the mid-points of the legs, vertical reactions N up at both feet.
_note: Two things about the printed figure. (1) It marks the right leg in TWO segments, apex-to-cross-bar labelled '1m' and cross-bar-to-floor labelled '1m', which reads as a 2 m leg and contradicts the stem's 'Each leg is 1 m long' and the solution's L = 1 m with the cross bar at L/2. The final answer is unaffected because L cancels out of N.L.sin20 = T.(L/2).cos20, giving T = 2N tan20. (2) The book sets the degree sign as a superscript zero (20^0, 40^0); transcribed here as 20 degrees / 40 degrees. Arithmetic checked: tan 20 = 0.3640, so 2 x 250 x 0.364 = 182 N, consistent.

stem:
A letter 'E' is prepared from a uniform cardboard with shape and dimensions as shown in the figure. Locate its centre of mass.

[Figure: the letter E is 3 cm wide and 5 cm tall and is made up of ten 1 cm squares whose centres are marked with dots numbered 1 to 10. The top arm is the row of three squares 1, 2, 3; below it the single square 4 continues the vertical spine; the middle arm is the pair of squares 5 and 6 (two squares wide only); below that the single square 7 continues the spine; and the bottom arm is the row of three squares 8, 9, 10. A brace marks the 1 cm height of the middle arm.]
solution:
As the sheet is uniform, each square can be taken to be equivalent to mass \(m\) concentrated at its respective centre. These masses will then be at the points labelled with numbers 1 to 10, as shown in figure. Let us select the origin to be at the left central mass \(m_5\), as shown and all the co-ordinates to be in cm.

By symmetry, the centre of mass of \(m_1\), \(m_2\) and \(m_3\) will be at \(m_2\ \left(1,\ 2\right)\) having effective mass \(3m\). Similarly, effective mass \(3m\) due to \(m_8\), \(m_9\) and \(m_{10}\) will be at \(m_9\ \left(1,\ -2\right)\). Again, by symmetry, the centre of mass of these two (\(3m\) each) will have co-ordinates \(\left(1,\ 0\right)\). Mass \(m_6\) is also having co-ordinates \(\left(1,\ 0\right)\). Thus, the effective mass at \(\left(1,\ 0\right)\) is \(7m\).

Using symmetry for \(m_4\), \(m_5\) and \(m_7\), there will be effective mass \(3m\) at the origin \(\left(0,\ 0\right)\).

Thus, effectively, \(3m\) and \(7m\) are separated by 1 cm along \(x\)-direction. \(y\)-coordinate is not required.

\(x_c = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{3 \times 0 + 7 \times 1}{3 + 7} = 0.7\ \text{cm}\)

Alternately, for two point masses, the centre of mass divides the distance between them in the inverse ratio of their masses. Hence, 1 cm is divided in the ratio 7:3. \(\therefore x_c = \dfrac{7}{7 + 3} \times 1 = 0.7\ \text{cm}\) from \(3m\), i.e., from the origin at \(m_c\)
diagramNote: The letter E as a 3 cm x 5 cm grid of ten 1 cm squares with their centres dotted and numbered 1-10 (top arm 1,2,3; spine square 4; middle arm 5,6; spine square 7; bottom arm 8,9,10).
_note: The stem gives no dimensions in words at all - the shape, the 3 cm x 5 cm envelope and the numbering 1..10 exist only in the figure, so the question is unanswerable without it; the figure is therefore described inside the stem. Also, the closing phrase prints 'from the origin at \(m_c\)' with a lowercase-c subscript, but the origin was defined at \(m_5\) and no mass \(m_c\) exists in this problem - transcribed as printed. All arithmetic checks out (3m at (0,0), 7m at (1,0), x_c = 0.7 cm).

stem: Three thin walled uniform hollow spheres of radii 1cm, 2 cm and 3 cm are so located that their centres are on the three vertices of an equilateral triangle ABC having each side 10 cm. Determine centre of mass of the system.
solution:
Mass of a thin walled uniform hollow sphere is proportional to its surface area, (as density is constant) hence proportional to \(r^2\). Thus, if mass of the sphere at A is \(m_{\text{A}} = m\), then \(m_{\text{B}} = 4m\) and \(m_{\text{C}} = 9m\). By symmetry of the spherical surface, their centres of mass are at their respective centres, i.e., at A, B and C.

[Figure: the equilateral triangle ABC of side 10 cm, drawn with A at the top apex carrying the sphere of radius 1 cm and mass \(m\), B at the bottom-right vertex carrying the sphere of radius 2 cm and mass \(4m\), and C at the bottom-left vertex carrying the sphere of radius 3 cm and mass \(9m\). The 10 cm separation of the two lower centres is marked.]

Let us choose the origin to be at C, where the largest mass \(9m\) is located and the point B with mass \(4m\) on the positive \(x\)-axis. With this, the co-ordinates of C are \(\left(0,\ 0\right)\) and that of B are \(\left(10,\ 0\right)\). (Locating the origin at the larger mass here save our efforts of calculations like multiplications with larger numbers). If A of mass \(m\) is taken in the first quadrant, its co-ordinates will be \(\left[5,\ \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]\)

\(x_c = \dfrac{m_{\text{A}}x_{\text{A}} + m_{\text{B}}x_{\text{B}} + m_{\text{C}}x_{\text{C}}}{m_{\text{A}} + m_{\text{B}} + m_{\text{C}}}\)

\(= \dfrac{m \times 5 + 4m \times 10 + 9m \times 0}{m + 4m + 9m} = \dfrac{45}{14}\ \text{cm}\)

\(y_c = \dfrac{m_{\text{A}}y_{\text{A}} + m_{\text{B}}y_{\text{B}} + m_{\text{C}}y_{\text{C}}}{m_{\text{A}} + m_{\text{B}} + m_{\text{C}}}\)

\(= \dfrac{m \times \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{2} + 4m \times 0 + 9m \times 0}{m + 4m + 9m} = \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{28}\ \text{cm}\)
diagramNote: Equilateral triangle ABC of side 10 cm; hollow spheres of radii 1 cm at A (top), 2 cm at B (bottom right) and 3 cm at C (bottom left), labelled with masses m, 4m and 9m.
_note: The stem does not say which radius sits on which vertex; that assignment (1 cm at A, 2 cm at B, 3 cm at C) comes only from the figure, and the solution depends on it. Arithmetic checked and consistent: the apex of an equilateral triangle of side 10 is at (5, 5*sqrt(3)) = (5, 10*sqrt(3)/2); x_c = 45/14 cm and y_c = 5*sqrt(3)/14 = 10*sqrt(3)/28 cm.

stem: A hole of radius \(r\) is cut from a uniform disc of radius \(2r\). Centre of the hole is at a distance \(r\) from centre of the disc. Locate centre of mass of the remaining part of the disc.
solution:
**Method I:** (Using entire disc): Before cutting the hole, c.m. of the full disc was at its centre. Let this be our origin O. Centre of mass of the cut portion is at its centre D. Thus, it is at a distance \(x_1 = r\) form the origin. Let C be the centre of mass of the remaining disc. Obviously, it should be on the extension of the line DO. Let it be at a distance \(x_2 = x\) from the origin. As the disc is uniform, mass of any of its part is proportional to the area of that part.

[Figure: the full disc of radius \(2r\) is shaded, with its centre O; the circular hole of radius \(r\) is drawn inside it with its centre D at a distance \(r\) to the right of O (so the hole touches the rim). The remaining shaded portion is labelled mass \(= 3m\), and the point C, the centre of mass of the remaining part, is marked to the LEFT of O.]

Thus, if \(m\) is the mass of the cut disc, mass of the entire disc must be \(4m\) and mass of the remaining disc will be \(3m\).

\(x_c = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}\)  As centre of mass of the full disc is at the origin, we can write,

\(0 = \dfrac{m \times r + 3m \times \left(x\right)}{m + 3m}\)  \(\therefore x = \dfrac{-r}{3}\)

**Method II:** (Using negative mass): Let \(\vec{R}\) be the position vector of the centre of mass of the uniform disc of mass \(M\). Mass \(m\) is with centre of mass at position vector \(\vec{r}\) from the centre of the disc. Position vector of the centre of mass of the remaining disc is then given by

\(\vec{r}_c = \dfrac{M\vec{R} - m\vec{r}}{M - m}\) ..... (as if there is a negative mass, i.e., \(m_2 = -m\))

With our description, \(M = 4m\), \(m = m\), \(R = 0\) and \(r = r\)  \(\therefore r_c = \dfrac{-mr}{3m} = \dfrac{-r}{3}\) ... Same as method I.
diagramNote: Shaded disc of radius 2r centred at O with a circular hole of radius r centred at D, r to the right of O; the remaining shaded part labelled mass = 3m and its centre of mass C marked to the left of O.
_note: The printed text has the misprint 'at a distance x1 = r form the origin' (form for from); transcribed as printed. Both methods are internally consistent and agree on x = -r/3.

A uniform rod of mass \(2m\) is held horizontal by two sturdy, practically inextensible vertical strings tied at its ends. A boy of mass \(3m\) hangs himself at one third length of the rod. Ratio of the tension in the string close to the boy to that in the other string is
Select WRONG statement about centre of mass:

options.label: A
options.text: Centre of mass of a 'C' shaped uniform rod can never be a point on that rod.

options.label: B
options.text: If the line of action of a force passes through the centre of mass, the moment of that force is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Centre of mass of our Earth is not at its geometrical centre.

options.label: D
options.text: While balancing an object on a pivot, the line of action of the gravitational force of the earth passes through the centre of mass of the object.

_note: Derived against the chapter's own 'Characteristics of centre of mass' list (section 4.13.4, p-25/p-26), which endorses the other three options almost verbatim and so isolates (C) as the WRONG statement: characteristic 16 plus the following text ('Centre of mass need not be within the body ... Other examples are a ring, a horse shoe, etc.') supports (A); characteristic 4 ('Centre of mass is the point at which, if a force is applied, it causes only linear acceleration and not angular acceleration') supports (B); characteristic 11 ('While balancing an object on a pivot, the line of action of weight must pass through the centre of mass and the pivot') supports (D) almost word for word. Against that, characteristics 14 and 15 (centre of mass lies on an axis of symmetry, and at the intersection of multiple axes of symmetry) put the Earth's centre of mass AT its geometrical centre, making (C) false. Recorded because (B) is a tempting alternative: strictly, the moment of a force is zero only about a point on its line of action, so (B) is unqualified and false about an arbitrary axis - but it is true about the centre of mass, which is the sense the book's own characteristic 4 states.

stem:
For which of the following objects will the centre of mass NOT be at their geometrical centre?
(I) An egg
(II) a cylindrical box full of rice
(III) a cubical box containing assorted sweets
_note: Item (II) is the weak member and is recorded rather than smoothed over. (I) is certain - an egg is neither symmetric nor uniform, so its centre of mass is displaced towards the broader end. (III) is certain - 'assorted' sweets differ in size and density, so the filling is non-uniform. The only printed option containing BOTH of those certain members is (D), so (D) is the key; (A) drops (III) and (C) drops (I). That forces (II) to count as non-central too, which is defensible on the chapter's own criterion but not on a naive reading: characteristic 6 (section 4.13.4) says the centre of mass is at the geometrical centre only 'for a symmetric rigid body OF UNIFORM DENSITY' (the book's own emphasis), and a box of loose rice is neither a rigid body nor of strictly uniform density - discrete grains pack with random voids and compact slightly under their own weight, so the centre of mass sits marginally below the geometrical centre. If the rice is idealised as a uniform continuum filling a symmetric box, its centre of mass IS at the geometrical centre and the correct set would be (I) and (III) only, which no printed option carries.
